fields.v: Wang, Y., Jiang, Z., Wang, R., Gong, N. Z. (2026). Package Hallucination Attacks on Coding Agents through Prompt Injection in Rule Files. arXiv:2610.09264v1 [cs.CR], 7 Oct 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2610.09264v1 [cs.CR], 7 Oct 2026; no venue stated
Duke University, USA (all four authors)

Proposes an approach; secondary: Compares — package hallucination attack and PackHallu, an evolutionary optimizer of malicious prompts injected into rule files; attack success compared with 5 prompt-injection baselines and measured across 3 benchmarks, 8 agent frameworks, 13 LLMs; 5 detectors evaluated
fields.why: Form '<nature>; secondary: <nature> — <detail>' fixed. Secondary changed from Evaluates to Compares because PackHallu is compared with five baselines under the same setting (Table 2); either is defensible. Also unclear whether an attack counts as an 'approach' in the protocol's sense
fields.doubt: O PackHallu é um ataque, não uma abordagem de desenvolvimento. Decide se fica 'Proposes an approach' e se a natureza secundária é Compares (5 ataques de base, Tabela 2) ou Evaluates.

fields.v: PackHallu (attack framework; no version). Target artefact: coding rule files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules) shared via open-source platforms and marketplaces

Not a development approach. Artefacts: benign coding rule file with an injected malicious prompt (default at the beginning); attacker-controlled malicious package (interface-compatible, suffix _hl) on a local PyPI mirror

Attack: seed prompt -> evolutionary loop (surrogate agent simulated by an LLM produces trajectory; trajectory-level signal scores occurrences of malicious package; attack LLM self-attributed critique -> strategy -> rewrite of offspring; top-k selection) for R rounds -> best prompt injected into rule file -> victim agent loads rule file and generates code
None (victim agents run in autonomous mode with manual confirmation disabled)
Single artefact (rule/context file) as attack vector, loaded by real agent frameworks; no specification
Not classifiable (rule-file security attack, no specification); authors do not use SDD terms
New code (file-level code generation from scratch: BigCodeBench, DS-1000) and existing code base (repository-level multi-file refactoring: RefactorBench)

BigCodeBench 981 victim tasks (5 packages, 80% victim / 20% surrogate split), DS-1000 772 tasks (4 packages), RefactorBench 43 tasks (5 packages); 10 victim packages; Claude Code case study on 87 numpy tasks; detection benchmark 200 rule files (100 benign, 100 malicious)
Python; data science and general third-party packages (pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scipy, seaborn; kombu, twisted, urllib3, asgiref, werkzeug); software supply-chain security
N/A (no human participants)

None measured per configuration. Stated in the appendix: one PackHallu optimization run takes about 24-30 h on up to two NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 GPUs (24 GB); prompt optimized once per agent on the numpy pair 'to reduce computational cost'; 600 s timeout per victim task

SASR (share of tasks where malicious package imported) and DASR (malicious package imported and code executes, malicious behaviour triggered), computed only on tasks the agent solves correctly under benign conditions; agent capability score (share of executable correct solutions benign)
fields.why: SASR and DASR measure attack success (a security outcome), not functional quality of the generated code; only the agent capability score is a functional-quality metric. They could be moved to 'Other outcome metrics'
fields.doubt: SASR e DASR medem o sucesso do ataque (segurança), não a qualidade funcional do código. Decide se ficam aqui ou passam para 'Other outcome metrics', deixando só a capability.

Attention proportion on malicious prompt; correlation of success with package popularity (PyPI downloads) and agent capability; trajectory categories in Claude Code case study; detector FNR and FPR

Automatic: import detection in generated code, execution with print-based malicious behaviour from local PyPI mirror, attention extraction, detectors' outputs. Manual (presumably): categorization of 87 Claude Code trajectories (procedure Not stated)

Success criterion: no criterion stated by the authors (SASR/DASR on BigCodeBench reported; cost not measured for any configuration). (1) PackHallu + OpenHands + 5 backbones (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Qwen3-Coder-30B, Devstral-Small-2-24B, GLM4.7-Flash-30B, Gemma4-31B), same surrogate and victim: avg SASR 79.29%, DASR 67.68% (per package SASR 70.02-86.19%, DASR >56%). Quality: no criterion stated by the authors; cost: not measured. (2) Baselines in the same settings: Combined Attack avg SASR/DASR 14.99/11.35; Repeat, GCG, ObliInjection lower; TAP strongest baseline (e.g. Qwen3-Coder-30B Pandas 34.62/26.92 vs PackHallu 98.72/89.74). Quality: no criterion stated by the authors; cost: not measured. (3) Transfer to other backbones on OpenHands (12 LLMs incl. GPT-5.5, GPT-5.3-Codex, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Llama-4-Maverick): >90% SASR on >=3 of 5 packages for 8 of 12; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B 22.73-50.00% SASR, 7.89-26.47% DASR. No criterion stated by the authors. (4) Transfer to other frameworks with Qwen3-Coder-30B (OpenCode, Aider, Pi, Cline, Kilo Code): avg SASR 71.55%, DASR 62.99%. No criterion stated by the authors. (5) Claude Code 2.1.141 + Claude Sonnet 4.6: SASR 31.03-58.95%, DASR 31.03-57.89% (most resistant). No criterion stated by the authors. (6) Cursor + Auto: SASR 69.35-98.00%; Cursor + Composer 2.5: 81.40-95.65%; OpenCode + DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 75.32-93.94%; average of the four agents in (5)-(6) SASR 74.81%, DASR 65.38%. No criterion stated by the authors. (7) Dataset transfer: DS-1000 SASR 53.33 / DASR 45.00; RefactorBench 18.60 / 16.28. No criterion stated by the authors. Ablations: injection location (OpenCode + DeepSeek-V4-Flash, stated): beginning avg SASR 82.63 vs 74.03 middle, 77.29 end; initializations (setting not stated; default row 97.50/97.50 matches OpenHands + Qwen3-Coder-30B on Seaborn in Table 2): default + 4 paraphrased prompts 98.00±2.09 SASR, 96.00±1.37 DASR; components (setting not stated; full row 83.87/50.54 matches OpenCode + DeepSeek-V4-Flash on Pandas): w/o trajectory-level signal 56.99/24.73, w/o self-attributed critique 62.37/47.31, w/o strategy proposal 63.44/46.24; hyperparameters (same setting): rounds 10/20/30 SASR 75.27/83.87/84.95, top-k 1/5/10 43.01/83.87/80.65, offspring 1/3/5 56.99/83.87/86.02, surrogate tasks 1/10/20 21.50/83.87/87.10. No criterion stated by the authors
fields.why: Ablation entries wrongly attributed to OpenCode + DeepSeek-V4-Flash: the paper states that setting only for the injection-location ablation; the initialization and component ablations give no setting (initialization default row matches OpenHands + Qwen3-Coder-30B). DASR values of the component ablation and the hyperparameter ablation (Table 11) were missing

fields.v: Tasks: BigCodeBench (main), DS-1000, RefactorBench adapted by package. Configurations: PackHallu vs 5 prompt-injection baselines (Combined, Repeat, GCG and ObliInjection with white-box advantage, TAP with same surrogate); 8 frameworks x 13 LLMs for transfer. Held constant: rule-file loading per framework recommendation, autonomous mode, injection position, local PyPI mirror, single prompt optimized on numpy pair reused for all packages. Acceptance: execution and import checks. Repetitions: Not stated (single runs apparently; std only for initialization ablation). Human intervention: none (autonomous)

PackHallu outperforms all baselines on all packages and victim agents: avg 79.29/67.68 vs Combined Attack 14.99/11.35 (5.29x SASR, 5.96x DASR), the only baseline average the authors give (they call it the 'subpotimal' baseline). TAP is the strongest baseline in Table 2 (e.g. Qwen3-Coder-30B Pandas 34.62/26.92, GLM4.7-Flash-30B Pandas 87.64/86.59 vs PackHallu 98.72/89.74 and 91.01/73.17), but no average or ratio is reported for it. More capable backbones more vulnerable (r=0.785 for SASR vs capability); no relation across frameworks (r=-0.186). Popular packages harder to attack (median r=-0.69 SASR, -0.60 DASR). No significance tests. Detectors (FNR/FPR): ProtectAI-DeBERTa 100%/3%; PromptGuard 46%/5%; DataSentinel 49%/16%; PromptArmor 20%/34%; PIShield 21%/11%
fields.why: Combined Attack is not the best baseline: TAP is clearly stronger in Table 2, and the 5.29x/5.96x ratios are only against Combined; also added ProtectAI-DeBERTa FPR (3%) and the DASR popularity correlation

fields.v: Distinguished attacks clearly (large gaps). Repeatability: initialization ablation shows stability; repetitions per configuration not stated; no statistical tests. Authors state no limitations of the comparison method
No limitations section. Gaps: robust defences for the collaborative rule-file pipeline; existing detectors inadequate; attack weaker at repository level (RefactorBench)

Tables 2, 4-6, 8, 11 flattened by pdftotext into row runs; values mapped by column order (Table 2 rows per attack in order Combined, Repeat, GCG, ObliInjection, TAP, PackHallu; pairs SASR/DASR per LLM); check against PDF. Attack evaluated in a controlled simulation (local PyPI mirror; benign print payload). Code or data release: Not stated. Pre-registration: not claimed. Language: Python. Security paper: rule files as an attack surface, relevant to context-file artefacts only. Reporting inconsistencies: Combined Attack is called the 'subpotimal' baseline (p. 12) although TAP is higher in nearly every cell of Table 2; ablation Tables 9-11 do not state the agent/model setting (inferred from matching rows); component ablation said to have a 'significantly positive effect' (p. 18) without any statistical test
fields.why: Missing reporting inconsistencies: 'subpotimal' baseline claim contradicted by Table 2 (TAP), unstated ablation settings, and 'significantly' claimed without tests

fields.doubt: O artigo indica 2 GPUs RTX 6000 e 24-30 h por otimização (p. 23), mas é um ataque, não uma abordagem para equipas. Decide entre Partly, Yes ou N/A.
